{"id": "7b8a41f9-4a7b-4094-a111-4292d051d071", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_f4TpG0OtBj4XNfh1pwkxOy", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot the \\\"ThrottlingException\\\" error when I use Amazon Bedrock on-demand resources?\",\"context\":\"### Request a quota increase\\n\\nNew AWS accounts might have lower initial quotas than the default quotas. Specific models have non-adjustable fixed quotas. If your workload traffic exceeds your account's on-demand quotas, then contact [AWS Support](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awssupport/latest/user/case-management.html#creating-a-support-case) or your account manager to [request a quota increase](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-increase.html). AWS might adjust default quotas based on usage patterns or service requirements.\\n\\nInclude the following information in your request:\\n\\n* The name of the quota to increase\\n* Your current quota value and the quota value that you require\\n* The model ID\\n* The Region for the quota increase\\n* A brief explanation of your use case\\n* Your projected usage, including steady and peak tokens and requests per minute, and average input and output tokens per request\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-throttling-error\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Quotas for the bedrock-mantle endpoint\",\"context\":\"## How requests are evaluated against quotas\\n\\nWhen you submit an inference request to the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint, AWS evaluates it against your quotas in the following order:\\n\\n1. **Input tokens per minute** \u2013 The number of input tokens in the request, plus the value of `max_tokens` (or the model-specific maximum if `max_tokens` is not set), is checked against the input-tokens-per-minute quota for the requested model. If admitting the request would exceed the quota, the request is throttled with an HTTP 429 response.\\n2. **Output tokens per minute** \u2013 As the model streams or generates output, output tokens are counted against the output-tokens-per-minute quota for that model. If the quota is reached during generation, generation stops and the response is returned with a finish reason indicating the cutoff.\\n\\nAfter the response completes, any unused portion of the initial input-token reservation (the difference between `max_tokens` and the actual output) is replenished to your quota.\\n\\nThe endpoint may apply additional internal rate limiting that is not exposed in Service Quotas. Use retry logic with exponential backoff to handle transient throttling.\\n\\nThe `bedrock-runtime` endpoint's TPM quotas count input and output tokens together against a single per-model quota, while the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint applies separate input-tokens-per-minute and output-tokens-per-minute quotas. If you run workloads on both endpoints, plan capacity for each endpoint independently. For details on the runtime endpoint's quotas, see Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-mantle.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"bedrockruntime\",\"context\":\"## type ThrottlingException \\n\\n```\\ntype ThrottlingException struct {\\n RespMetadata protocol.ResponseMetadata `json:\\\"-\\\" xml:\\\"-\\\"`\\n\\n Message_ *string `locationName:\\\"message\\\" type:\\\"string\\\"`\\n // contains filtered or unexported fields\\n}\\n```\\n\\nYour request was throttled because of service-wide limitations. Resubmit\\nyour request later or in a different region. You can also purchase Provisioned\\nThroughput (<https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html>)\\nto increase the rate or number of tokens you can process\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-go/api/service/bedrockruntime/index.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Scaling and throughput best practices\",\"context\":\"## Ramping up throughput\\n\\nOn-demand capacity can vary by model, Region, and time. Not all requests within a quota are guaranteed to succeed during periods of high demand, so ramp gradually when launching a workload, changing models or Regions, or making a large traffic increase. This is especially important for `bedrock-mantle` models that do not have a published per-account quota.\\n\\n### Recommended ramp-up procedure\\n\\n1. Estimate the target token rate and concurrency for each endpoint, model, and Region. For `bedrock-mantle`, track input and output tokens separately and include the requested `max_tokens` value in the input-token admission estimate.\\n2. Begin at a known stable baseline below the target. If you do not have a baseline, start with a small representative load instead of sending the full target volume.\\n3. Hold each level long enough to observe request success, 429/503/529 errors, latency percentiles, token consumption, concurrency, and queue depth.\\n4. Increase one controlled step at a time. Change only one major load dimension at a time so that you can identify the cause of a regression.\\n5. If throttling, capacity errors, or latency rise beyond your threshold, pause the ramp, honor any `Retry-After` header, and return to the last stable level.\\n6. Continue until you reach the target, and repeat the validation for every model and Region that will receive production traffic.\\n\\nChoose the step size and observation period from your workload's latency and traffic pattern. Do not use RPM as the only control signal: request token sizes and response lengths can change capacity consumption substantially even when RPM stays constant.\\n\\nFor `bedrock-mantle` quota increases, follow Requesting a quota increase. For `bedrock-runtime`, follow Requesting a quota increase\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/scaling-throughput-best-practices.html\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock\",\"context\":\"## Understanding token quota management\\n\\nWhen you make a request, tokens are deducted from your TPM and TPD quotas.\\nCalculations occur at the following stages:\\n\\n* **At the start of the request** \u2013 The\\n following sum is deducted from your quotas. The request is throttled if you\\n exceed a quota.\\n\\n ```\\n Total input tokens + max_tokens\\n ```\\n* **During processing** \u2013 The quota\\n consumed by the request is periodically adjusted to account for the actual\\n number of output tokens generated.\\n* **At the end of the request** \u2013 The\\n total number of tokens consumed by the request will be calculated as follows and any unused tokens are replenished to your quota:\\n\\n ```\\n InputTokenCount + CacheWriteInputTokenCount + (OutputTokenCount x burndown rate)\\n ```\\n\\n `CacheReadInputTokenCount` don't contribute to this calculation and are not counted toward your quota. If you don't use prompt caching, both `CacheWriteInputTokenCount` and `CacheReadInputTokenCount` will be 0.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nYou're only billed for your actual token usage.\\n\\nFor example, if you use Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4 and send a request containing 1,000 input tokens and it generates a response equivalent to 100 tokens:\\n\\n* **1,500 tokens** (1,000 + 100 x 5) will be depleted from your TPM and TPD quotas.\\n* You'll only be billed for **1,100 tokens**\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search Bedrock docs on quota increases and throttling"}

{"id": "1d6f3149-3ce5-4e86-bea9-38d90ef1a4e0", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_V9CQzDN1kQabCsiunul3Je", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Capacity and Performance\",\"context\":\"## Limits & Quotas\\n\\n### On-Demand Limits (by tier)\\n\\n| Tier | RPM Range | TPM Range | Throttling Risk |\\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\\n| Flex | 10-100 | 5K-50K | High |\\n| Standard | 100-500 | 50K-150K | Medium |\\n| Priority | 500-1000+ | 150K-300K+ | Low |\\n\\n* Burst capacity: Available across all tiers for short spikes\\n* Soft limits: Increasable through service quota requests\\n* Model-specific: Actual limits vary by foundation model\\n\\n### Reserved Tier Limits\\n\\n* Minimum commitment: 1 model unit\\n* Maximum units: Account and region-specific\\n* Input/output token limits: Based on purchased units\\n* No RPM throttling within purchased capacity\\n\\n### Batch Processing Limits\\n\\n* Job size and file size: Quotas for records per job, records per input file, input file size, and job size vary by model. For current values, see the batch inference quotas in Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas in the AWS General Reference.\\n* Processing time: On-demand requests are prioritized over batch jobs, so processing time depends on available capacity. Completion is not guaranteed. Each job has a timeout, 24 hours by default and up to 168 hours, that you set with the `timeoutDurationInHours` field of CreateModelInvocationJob.\\n* Concurrent jobs: Region-specific quotas\\n\\n### Cross-Region Inference\\n\\n* Inherits on-demand tier limits per region\\n* No additional quota overhead\\n* Automatic routing (no manual limit management)\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/capacity-limits-cost-optimization.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Global cross-Region inference\",\"context\":\"## Global cross-Region inference considerations\\n\\nNote the following information about Global cross-Region inference:\\n\\n* For default cross-Region throughput quotas when using Global\\n inference profiles, see the **Global Cross-region\\n model inference requests per minute for ${Model}** and\\n **Global Cross-region model inference tokens per\\n minute for ${Model}** values in Amazon Bedrock service\\n quotas in the *AWS General\\n Reference*.\\n\\n You can request, view, and manage quotas for the Global Cross-Region\\n Inference Profile from the Service Quotas console or by using AWS CLI commands in your\\n **source region**\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/global-cross-region-inference.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Costs and throughput\",\"context\":\"# Costs and throughput\\n\\nA function that invokes a model calls Amazon Bedrock in your account, with your credentials.\\nThat means:\\n\\n* The model charges appear on your own Amazon Bedrock bill. AWS CloudTrail in your\\n account records each call under the feed's access role, in a role session named\\n `ei-function-feed-id`.\\n* Elemental Inference invokes the model in the feed's AWS Region. The invocations count against your\\n account's Amazon Bedrock quotas for that model in that Region. To use a model in other\\n Regions, specify a cross-Region inference profile ID as the function's\\n model.\\n* Your account must be able to invoke the model in that Region before the function\\n can run. Elemental Inference doesn't enable model access on your behalf.\\n\\nImportant\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nOn-demand Amazon Bedrock throughput is shared across everything in your account that uses\\nthat model. A function on a live feed fires continuously for as long as the channel\\nruns, which is the workload that exhausts an on-demand quota and starts\\nthrottling your other applications. For a production feed, use provisioned throughput\\nfor the model, or a cross-Region inference profile, and size it for the cadence you\\nconfigured. For more information, see Increase throughput with\\nprovisioned throughput in the *Amazon Bedrock User Guide*.\\n\\nA passthrough function invokes no model, so it incurs no model charges and consumes no\\nAmazon Bedrock quota.\\n\\nFor more information about Elemental Inference pricing, see Pricing for AWS Elemental Inference\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elemental-inference/latest/userguide/functions-costs.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Scaling and throughput best practices\",\"context\":\"## `bedrock-runtime` endpoint: throughput and quotas\\n\\nThe `bedrock-runtime` endpoint has the following quota behavior:\\n\\n* Per-model, per-Region token quotas count input and output tokens together. Output tokens consume quota according to a model-specific burndown rate.\\n* Some models also have RPM quotas, while other models are governed only by token quotas. Check the quotas that apply to the exact model and inference profile that you use.\\n* Per-minute and per-day token quotas are shared across the inference APIs that call the same model on this endpoint. Allocations for `bedrock-runtime` and `bedrock-mantle` are independent.\\n* Custom inference profiles, batch inference, and Provisioned Throughput have separate quotas and are available only through `bedrock-runtime`.\\n\\nFor current quota values, token-burndown details, and the quota-increase process, see Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint. See the applicable Models at a glance for model-specific endpoint, service-tier, and feature support\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/scaling-throughput-best-practices.html\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"amazon-bedrock\",\"skill_description\":\"Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation (Converse API, InvokeModel), RAG with Knowledge Bases, Bedrock Agents, Guardrails, and AgentCore (including the Harness managed agent loop). Applies when invoking models, setting up or migrating Knowledge Bases to Managed, deploying to AgentCore, migrating/porting/converting a Bedrock Agent (including inline agents) to an AgentCore Harness, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing Bedrock models (Claude, Llama, Nova, Titan). Also for prompt caching, quota and throttling diagnosis, cost tracking, migrating between Claude model generations, chunking strategies, and Bedrock model selection. Covers AgentCore Payments (x402, microtransactions, Payment Manager, Connector, Instrument, Coinbase CDP, Stripe Privy, paid endpoints, agent payments). NOT for custom model training, Rekognition, or Comprehend. For SageMaker model discovery, customization, or endpoints, use aws-ai-ml.\\n\\nServices: bedrock, bedrock-runtime, bedrock-mantle, bedrock-agent, bedrock-agent-runtime, bedrock-agentcore-control, bedrock-agentcore\\nTasks: deploy, debug, optimize, design, migrate\\nPersona: developer, devops, architect\\nWorkload: generative-ai, rag, agents\",\"skill_name\":\"amazon-bedrock\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search Bedrock docs on cross-region inference and provisioned throughput"}

{"id": "e87491a2-b149-4a70-9b1b-2282d9462cb5", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "In most cases, start with the cheap options and request a quota increase. Buy Provisioned Throughput only if your peak is steady and predictable, or if you need guaranteed capacity.

**Why a quota increase usually comes first**
- It costs nothing extra. You keep paying per token.
- Quotas are per model and per Region. Tokens per minute (TPM) counts input and output together, and output tokens are weighted by a model-specific burndown rate. In the docs' Claude Sonnet 4 example, 1,000 input and 100 output tokens use 1,500 TPM but are billed as 1,100.
- Each request also reserves `input tokens + max_tokens` up front, and the unused part is refunded afterward. An oversized `max_tokens` can cause throttling well below your real usage.
- AWS asks for the following in the request:
  - the quota name
  - your current and required values
  - the model ID and Region
  - your use case
  - steady and peak TPM and RPM
  - average input and output tokens per request

  A request with solid numbers gets approved more often.
- Quota approval isn't a capacity guarantee. The docs say on-demand capacity varies by model, Region and time, and requests within quota can still be throttled during high demand.

**When Provisioned Throughput makes sense**
- You have a sustained, predictable peak, and the commitment's hourly cost beats paying per token at that volume.
- You need guaranteed capacity with no throttling within what you buy. The docs describe reserved capacity as having no RPM throttling within purchased units.
- You use a custom or fine-tuned model, which runs on Provisioned Throughput.
- The trade-off is that you pay for the capacity whether or not you use it. If you peak for a few hours a day, it's usually expensive. Not every model supports it, so check your model and Region first.

**Things to try first, or alongside either option**
1. **Cross-Region inference profiles.** A geographic or global profile spreads load across Regions and often raises your effective TPM. Global profile quotas are managed in Service Quotas in your source Region.
2. **Lower `max_tokens`** to what you actually need, so each request reserves less quota.
3. **Prompt caching.** Cache reads don't count toward your quota.
4. **Retries with exponential backoff and jitter**, plus request queueing, to smooth short bursts.
5. **Move non-urgent work to batch inference**, which has separate quotas, so it doesn't compete with interactive traffic at peak.

**Suggested path**
1. Check how often you're throttled and how close your usage runs to the quota.
2. Apply the quick wins above.
3. Request a quota increase, and use a cross-Region profile if it fits your latency and data-residency needs.
4. If you're still throttled, or you need guaranteed capacity, price Provisioned Throughput against your sustained peak.
